items.primary_i_can: I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.
items.evidence_job: Navigate a connected physics-evidence stimulus by identifying what is observable, what is inferred, what evidence matters, and how a simple relationship/model could organize the reasoning.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.1: observations/evidence/testability/model-or-formula interpretation; Physics Framework: conceptual meaning before calculation.
items.student_text:
A class tests the claim: ‘A larger pull on the same spring produces a larger stretch.’ They record:

Pull force (N) | Spring stretch (cm)
2 | 1.1
4 | 2.0
6 | 3.2
8 | 4.1

(a) State one observation from the table and one inference a student could make from it.
(b) Does the evidence support the claim? Cite a specific pattern.
(c) A student sketches the relationship as stretch ∝ pull force. Explain what that relationship tells you physically without calculating a new value.
(d) Name one additional measurement or repeated trial that would make the evidence stronger.
items.student_html:
A class tests the claim: ‘A larger pull on the same spring produces a larger stretch.’ They record:

Pull force (N) | Spring stretch (cm)
2 | 1.1
4 | 2.0
6 | 3.2
8 | 4.1

(a) State one observation from the table and one inference a student could make from it.
(b) Does the evidence support the claim? Cite a specific pattern.
(c) A student sketches the relationship as stretch ∝ pull force. Explain what that relationship tells you physically without calculating a new value.
(d) Name one additional measurement or repeated trial that would make the evidence stronger.
items.answer: (a) Example observation: the measured stretch is 1.1 cm at 2 N. Example inference: stronger pulls cause larger stretches. (b) Yes; every increase in pull force is accompanied by an increase in stretch. (c) The relationship says stretch changes in the same direction as pull force for this spring; it organizes the pattern rather than serving only as an arithmetic rule. (d) Repeat each force several times or add additional force levels.
items.solution_text: The table contains directly observed measurements. An inference interprets the pattern. Because all four measurements rise together, the claim is supported by this data set, though repeated trials would strengthen the evidence. The proportional-style relationship summarizes how the two measured quantities are connected.
items.solution_html: The table contains directly observed measurements. An inference interprets the pattern. Because all four measurements rise together, the claim is supported by this data set, though repeated trials would strengthen the evidence. The proportional-style relationship summarizes how the two measured quantities are connected.

items.primary_i_can: I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.
items.evidence_job: Classify closely related evidence statements using the scientific-term distinctions, with a brief reason tied to the definition.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.1: observations/evidence/testability/model-or-formula interpretation; Physics Framework: conceptual meaning before calculation.
items.student_text: During a cooling-water test, a student writes: ‘The thermometer reads 18.4 °C,’ then writes, ‘The water cooled because the room was cold.’ Classify each statement as observation or inference and explain the distinction.
items.student_html: During a cooling-water test, a student writes: ‘The thermometer reads 18.4 °C,’ then writes, ‘The water cooled because the room was cold.’ Classify each statement as observation or inference and explain the distinction.
items.answer: 18.4 °C is an observation; the cause statement is an inference.
items.solution_text: The thermometer reading is directly measured. The proposed cause interprets why the measurement occurred, so it is an inference.
items.solution_html: The thermometer reading is directly measured. The proposed cause interprets why the measurement occurred, so it is an inference.

items.primary_i_can: I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.
items.evidence_job: Classify closely related evidence statements using the scientific-term distinctions, with a brief reason tied to the definition.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.1: observations/evidence/testability/model-or-formula interpretation; Physics Framework: conceptual meaning before calculation.
items.student_text: A motion sensor records a cart speed of 0.62 m/s. A student says, ‘The cart is slowing because the wheels are rubbing.’ Classify the measured statement and the causal statement.
items.student_html: A motion sensor records a cart speed of 0.62 m/s. A student says, ‘The cart is slowing because the wheels are rubbing.’ Classify the measured statement and the causal statement.
items.answer: 0.62 m/s is an observation; the rubbing explanation is an inference.
items.solution_text: A measured sensor value is an observation. The explanation about wheel rubbing goes beyond what was directly measured, so it is an inference.
items.solution_html: A measured sensor value is an observation. The explanation about wheel rubbing goes beyond what was directly measured, so it is an inference.

items.primary_i_can: I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.
items.evidence_job: Evaluate whether a proposed claim is scientifically testable and identify what observable or measurable evidence would make the test meaningful.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.1: observations/evidence/testability/model-or-formula interpretation; Physics Framework: conceptual meaning before calculation.
items.student_text: Claim: ‘A heavier pendulum bob always swings faster because heavy objects prefer downward motion.’ Is this claim scientifically testable as written? Revise it into a testable claim and name one measurement.
items.student_html: Claim: ‘A heavier pendulum bob always swings faster because heavy objects prefer downward motion.’ Is this claim scientifically testable as written? Revise it into a testable claim and name one measurement.
items.answer: Not adequately testable as written; a testable revision compares period for different bob masses while holding length constant and measures swing period.
items.solution_text: Scientific claims need observable consequences. A measurable revision is: with pendulum length fixed, changing bob mass changes the period. Measure the period for several masses.
items.solution_html: Scientific claims need observable consequences. A measurable revision is: with pendulum length fixed, changing bob mass changes the period. Measure the period for several masses.

items.primary_i_can: I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.
items.evidence_job: Evaluate whether a proposed claim is scientifically testable and identify what observable or measurable evidence would make the test meaningful.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.1: observations/evidence/testability/model-or-formula interpretation; Physics Framework: conceptual meaning before calculation.
items.student_text: Claim: ‘Magnets know when another magnet is nearby.’ Explain why this is not a useful scientific claim as written. Rewrite it so a class could test it and identify a measurement.
items.student_html: Claim: ‘Magnets know when another magnet is nearby.’ Explain why this is not a useful scientific claim as written. Rewrite it so a class could test it and identify a measurement.
items.answer: ‘Know’ is not operationally observable; revise to a measurable claim such as decreasing magnet separation increases measured magnetic force, then measure force and separation.
items.solution_text: A testable statement connects conditions to observable outcomes. Force versus separation can be measured, whereas ‘knowing’ cannot.
items.solution_html: A testable statement connects conditions to observable outcomes. Force versus separation can be measured, whereas ‘knowing’ cannot.

items.primary_i_can: I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.
items.evidence_job: Use evidence from a compact data/model representation to decide whether an explanation is supported and interpret what the relationship says physically.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.1: observations/evidence/testability/model-or-formula interpretation; Physics Framework: conceptual meaning before calculation.
items.student_text:
A cart is pushed with different forces while its motion change is rated on the same scale:
Force (N) | motion-change rating
2 | 1
4 | 2
6 | 3
8 | 4
A student claims that a larger applied force is associated with a larger change in motion. Is the claim supported? What does the pattern communicate physically?
items.student_html:
A cart is pushed with different forces while its motion change is rated on the same scale:
Force (N) | motion-change rating
2 | 1
4 | 2
6 | 3
8 | 4
A student claims that a larger applied force is associated with a larger change in motion. Is the claim supported? What does the pattern communicate physically?
items.answer: Yes; doubling the force doubles the rating in this data set. The table communicates that stronger applied forces are associated with larger motion changes under the tested conditions.
items.solution_text: The numerical pattern rises consistently: 2→1, 4→2, 6→3, 8→4. The relationship is a model of how the quantities co-vary, not merely numbers to substitute.
items.solution_html: The numerical pattern rises consistently: 2→1, 4→2, 6→3, 8→4. The relationship is a model of how the quantities co-vary, not merely numbers to substitute.

items.primary_i_can: I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.
items.evidence_job: Use evidence from a compact data/model representation to decide whether an explanation is supported and interpret what the relationship says physically.

items.student_text:
Students stretch the same elastic band:
Pull (N) | stretch (cm)
1 | 0.8
2 | 1.6
3 | 2.4
4 | 3.2
Does the evidence support the explanation that stretch grows with pull? Explain what the table says about the phenomenon.
items.student_html:
Students stretch the same elastic band:
Pull (N) | stretch (cm)
1 | 0.8
2 | 1.6
3 | 2.4
4 | 3.2
Does the evidence support the explanation that stretch grows with pull? Explain what the table says about the phenomenon.
items.answer: Yes; each additional 1 N is accompanied by 0.8 cm more stretch. The relationship summarizes a consistent increase in stretch as pull increases.
items.solution_text: The measured pairs form a regular increasing pattern, so the explanation is supported over the tested range.
items.solution_html: The measured pairs form a regular increasing pattern, so the explanation is supported over the tested range.

items.primary_i_can: I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.
items.evidence_job: Interpret a supplied physical relationship qualitatively before any arithmetic; connect variables to the phenomenon rather than treating the equation as a procedure.
items.source_basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.1: observations/evidence/testability/model-or-formula interpretation; Physics Framework: conceptual meaning before calculation.
items.student_text: A model says the distance traveled at constant speed is d = vt. Without calculating, predict what happens to distance if the travel time doubles while speed stays the same. Explain using the relationship.
items.student_html: A model says the distance traveled at constant speed is d = vt. Without calculating, predict what happens to distance if the travel time doubles while speed stays the same. Explain using the relationship.
items.solution_text: In d = vt, with v unchanged, d is directly proportional to t. Doubling t doubles the product and therefore the distance.
items.solution_html: In d = vt, with v unchanged, d is directly proportional to t. Doubling t doubles the product and therefore the distance.

items.student_text: For a constant-speed conveyor, d = vt. Without substituting numbers, predict how the distance changes if the speed is cut in half while the operating time stays fixed.
items.student_html: For a constant-speed conveyor, d = vt. Without substituting numbers, predict how the distance changes if the speed is cut in half while the operating time stays fixed.
items.solution_text: With t fixed, distance changes directly with speed. Halving v halves d.
items.solution_html: With t fixed, distance changes directly with speed. Halving v halves d.
